rationale: 702.26d is the rule that directly settles it: phasing isn't a zone change and zone-change triggers (which includes enters-the-battlefield triggers) don't trigger on phasing in or out. No other chunk is needed to answer it.

This is a true interaction: 702.19b says trample can only push excess past blockers after lethal damage is assigned, and 702.2c says any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that assignment. Neither half alone explains the result.

702.40a spells out that storm is a triggered ability worded 'When you cast this spell, copy it...', which is exactly what the question asks and implies it goes on the stack and can be countered (while the copies it makes are not themselves cast).

You need the deck-construction restriction (903.5c) plus something establishing that a hybrid symbol contributes both colors, which either the color identity definition (903.4, 'any mana symbols in that card's mana cost or rules text') or the hybrid symbol rule (107.4e, 'a hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors') supplies. Hence AND-of-ORs.
Both chunks independently state that no player receives priority during the untap step, so retrieving either one fully answers the question.
511.3 says creatures are removed from combat only as soon as the end of combat step ends, which is precisely the 'yes, they're still attacking during the step' answer.

305.1 and 116.2a each say the same thing from a different section: playing a land is a special action, it never uses the stack, and a land is never a spell. Either one answers 'no, you don't cast lands'.

702.74a gives evoke's actual template ('When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it'), which shows the sacrifice is a triggered ability that uses the stack and can therefore be responded to.

The question turns on keyword abilities being abilities at all; 702.1 and the Keyword Ability glossary entry each establish that a keyword is just shorthand for an ability, so losing all abilities removes them too.
402.2 says a player may have any number of cards in hand and only discards down during the cleanup step, so drawing at seven is fine; the glossary entry restates the same limit.
704.5i is the single state-based action covering a planeswalker with loyalty 0 being put into its owner's graveyard.

700.4 defines 'dies' as 'is put into a graveyard from the battlefield' with no creature restriction, which is the whole answer. The Dies glossary entry is deliberately excluded because it still says creature/planeswalker and would mislead.
The same rule is stated twice: 121.4 in the drawing section and 104.3c in the losing-the-game section both say you lose the next time a player would receive priority. Either is a correct hit.

Two-part question: 506.1 is the only chunk listing the five combat steps in order, and the defending player's priority comes from the priority chain, which either 117.3a (active player gets it first each step) or 117.3d (it passes to the next player in turn order) explains.
605.3b states outright that a mana ability can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to; 405.6c restates that mana abilities resolve immediately. Either answers 'no'.

Cost payment happens at 601.2h inside the uninterrupted casting process, and 601.2i is the point where the spell is actually cast and priority returns. You need both to see that there's no window to respond while costs are being paid.

613.1 introduces the layer ordering and 613.1a-g are the seven layers themselves; because the chunks are split per rule, surfacing any of them means the retriever found the layer system, which is what an open 'explain layers' question needs.
704.5j is the legend rule state-based action verbatim, and the Legend Rule glossary entry restates it. Either hit answers the question.

The 'when' is the point of the question: 704.5g is the lethal-damage destruction condition, and 704.3 supplies the timing (checked whenever a player would get priority, not the instant damage is marked). Incomplete without both.

The honest answer is 'not from exile itself, but you can move it': 903.9a lets the owner put a commander in exile into the command zone as a state-based action, and 903.8 is what permits casting it from there (with commander tax). Both pieces are required.

The cleanup step is exactly three things: discard to maximum hand size (514.1), remove damage and end 'until end of turn' effects (514.2), and normally no player gets priority (514.3). Missing any one leaves the answer incomplete.
704.3 and 117.5 describe the same check from the two sides (state-based actions and priority), each saying SBAs are performed whenever a player would get priority, before triggers go on the stack.
Three restatements of the same rule: a player may concede at any time and leaves the game immediately. Any single hit is a correct retrieval.
Glossary-kind question; 102.1 defines the active player as the player whose turn it is and the Active Player glossary entry says the same and points at 102.1.

117.3c says the player who had priority when they cast a spell receives priority afterward, so the nonactive caster keeps it rather than handing it to the active player; 601.2i restates this at the end of the casting process.
Same rule as the mirror question: under 117.3c (restated by 601.2i) the caster retains priority, so here the active player who cast the spell gets it back first.
Holding priority is just 117.3c: casting a spell hands priority straight back to you, so you can keep casting before anyone responds. 601.2i states the same thing inside the casting rules.

There are two separate times lore counters go on: the Saga enters with one (714.3a), and one is added as a turn-based action when its controller's precombat main phase begins (714.3c). Both are needed for a complete answer.
Glossary-kind definition question; 603.7 defines delayed triggered abilities and the glossary entry gives the same definition pointing at 603.7.
113.3a establishes spell abilities as the abilities of instant and sorcery spells, and 113.6 confirms instants and sorceries have abilities that function on the stack. Either chunk answers 'yes'.

702.61b says outright that players may activate mana abilities while a split second spell is on the stack, and 702.61a's wording ('can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities') carves out the same exception.
